title: Luckey Roberts as a person
summary: Roberts led small parties for the rich and treated Bauza like a son.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Since this is the last interview, I want to get into (unintelligible) things. Your first job was with Lucky Roberts. Can you remember anything about him? What kind of person was he when you worked with him? What did you do with him?

Lucky Roberts, I played some of these private parties for the rich people. He used to play a whole lot of them, sometimes four piece, sometimes five pieces. You know what I mean. He was a very nice man, because -- oh, man, he was a short guy. He always used to be racing all the time.
A whole lot of (unintelligible). All the time -- he played the piano with such a dynamic right hand, you know what I mean. So he played for all these rich people, played different parties for them.
What kind of -- when you say a quartet, what kind of instrumentation would he have?

(Unintelligible) might take a piano, might take me and the saxophone and might have a bass and a drum. Sometimes he might hire another -- he didn't want nothing too loud because it was in these private houses, you know what I mean.
He was a man in command of everything.
He was more like a __________, you know what I mean.
Everything was basic. His piano performance and his right hand -- sometimes, he'd sing in his own way, you know what I mean.
Do you remember any of the material he played?
Going so far back, you know what I mean, it's -- in those days, some of his own music, some of the Fats Waller music, some of the more modern music. That's what we used to play in those parties.
Okay. What was he like as a person?

Beautiful. Beautiful man. Very decent fellow. Very lovely fellow, lovely man. Very lovable man. He told me I was like his son, you know what I mean? He treated me like I was his son. I couldn't talk much then English, you know what I mean? But somehow we'd relate, one to the other, you know what I mean?
And he was a -- he always used to look for me, and his wife was a wonderful woman, too. Yeah, I really had a -- that was my first -- really, my first musical contact here in this country.
